title: Data story: what informal workers really value
gist: A World Bank report argues Latin America's stubborn 55% informality is not mainly exclusion: self-employed workers rationally choose informality for flexibility and autonomy, formal benefits act like a ~32% hidden tax on formality in some countries, and lasting reduction depends on productivity-led growth of larger formal firms, not registration simplification.

insights.claim: Latin America and the Caribbean has held roughly 55% of workers in informality for nearly two decades, a figure unchanged despite years of easier microenterprise registration, lower formal-hiring costs, and amnesty programs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Registration-simplification and hiring-cost policies have failed to move informality, signaling the standard policy toolkit is misdiagnosing the problem.
insights.quote: Latin America and the Caribbean has spent nearly two decades with 55% of its workers in informality.

insights.claim: Informality splits into informal wage workers, who are young with short tenure and show signs of exclusion, and the self-employed, who are older, stay for years, and follow a logic of rational choice.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Treating informality as one exclusionary block leads to wrong policies; the majority self-employed segment is a choice, not a failure to access formal jobs.
insights.quote: Being the boss of your own arepa stand may be preferred to the monotony of washing dishes as a salaried worker in a formal restaurant.

insights.claim: The informality rate ranges from 10% in Europe and Central Asia to 80% in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, placing Latin America's ~55% in the middle.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Informality scales inversely with development, framing it as a growth-stage phenomenon rather than a regional policy failure.

insights.claim: Informal wage employment declines steadily with age while informal self-employment grows with age, so the wage segment acts as a labor-market entry point and the self-employed segment as a durable destination.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Life-cycle dynamics mean interventions should differ by age and segment rather than applying uniform formalization pressure.
insights.locator: The different segments of the labor market

insights.claim: In a seven-country choice experiment (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru), self-employed workers valued flexibility and independence so highly they would give up as much as half their income to keep a job with those features.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The willingness to forgo up to 50% of income quantifies why wage subsidies alone cannot pull the self-employed into formal jobs.
insights.quote: they would be willing to give up as much as half their income to hold a job with these features.
insights.locator: 1. The value of being your own boss

insights.claim: Workers with high autonomy are willing to give up as much as 26% of their pay to keep it, and those with flexible hours value that flexibility almost three times more than those without it.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Non-wage job attributes carry large monetary value, which formal-sector job design ignores at its peril.
insights.quote: those with high autonomy are willing to give up as much as 26% of their pay to keep
insights.locator: 1. The value of being your own boss

insights.claim: Latin American microentrepreneurs are opportunity-driven 61% of the time, nearly as high as the OECD's 72%, behaving much like peers in developed countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Most microentrepreneurship is opportunity- not necessity-driven, undercutting the view that informality is purely survival behavior.
insights.quote: They are seeking an opportunity 61% of the times, nearly as high as the OECD's 72%.
insights.locator: 1. The value of being your own boss

insights.claim: The gap between what formal benefits cost and what workers value them at creates an implicit tax on formality of around 32% in Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, while in Chile the number is negative because workers value the benefits more than they cost.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A ~32% wedge makes formal hiring uncompetitive; redesigning benefits workers actually value is a higher-leverage reform than mandates.
insights.quote: an implicit tax on formality of around 32% in Brazil, Colombia, and Peru.

insights.claim: In Peru the cost of formal-work benefits, between employer payments and worker deductions, can reach 60% of the minimum wage, yet informal workers value them far below that cost.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The cost-valuation mismatch, partly from poor information and poorly serving benefits, is a concrete target for social-protection redesign.
insights.quote: In Peru, they can rea 60% of the minimum wage.

themes.theme: Growth, not registration, is the fix

insights.claim: Self-employment falls steadily as per-capita income rises, and Latin America today sits where Japan, South Korea, and Portugal were at the same income level, framing informality as a stage of development rather than an anomaly.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Convergence history implies informality shrinks with productivity-led growth, so growth policy is the durable lever, not formalization campaigns.
insights.quote: Latin America and the Caribbean is today where Japan, South Korea, and Portugal were when they had the same income level.

insights.claim: The biggest obstacle to good-job creation is the limited dynamism of larger formal firms, not the existence of informal microenterprises.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Policy should target productivity and growth of leading formal firms rather than penalizing or formalizing microenterprises.
insights.quote: The biggest obstacle to growth and the creation of good jobs is not the existence of informal microenterprises: it is the limited dynamism of those larger formal firms.
